analysis.one_liner: Requires regulators to consider labor standards when deciding which foreign airlines may fly into the US.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with one Republican cosponsor, it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes the standards the Transportation Department applies when deciding whether to grant a foreign airline permission to operate in the US. It requires regulators to consider whether the airline's practices undermine labor standards, such as basing crews in low-wage countries to avoid paying market wages, both in issuing permits and in shaping US international aviation negotiating policy. The idea is to prevent foreign airlines from competing against US carriers by hiring crews on terms US carriers could not match.
analysis.who_benefits: US airline pilots, flight attendants, and ground crews, who would face less competition from airlines that crew their flights cheaply by basing staff in low-wage countries; US carriers would also gain from a more level competitive field with carriers like those from the Gulf.

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'preventing the undermining of labor standards' to the factors the Transportation Department must weigh when deciding whether granting a foreign air carrier a permit to operate in the US is in the public interest.

Adds the same labor-standards factor to the policy the State and Transportation Departments must follow when negotiating US international air transportation agreements, so those deals would have to take labor into account.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign airlines that keep costs down by basing crews in low-wage countries could face higher labor costs, permit denials, or harder access to the US market; some of that cost could reach travelers as higher fares if competition narrows.

drawbacks.text: The bill could raise airfares for travelers by making it harder for lower-cost foreign carriers, or carriers with cheaper labor models, to compete in the US market.
Its terms are open-ended: 'preventing the undermining of labor standards' is not defined in the bill, which could invite inconsistent or politically driven permit decisions by regulators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real competitive and labor concern: foreign airlines can base crews in low-wage countries and undercut US carriers' labor costs while still flying into the US market. Weighing it honestly, the main cost would fall partly on travelers through reduced competition and possibly higher fares, and the vague labor-standards test gives regulators wide discretion. The benefit is wage protection for a large, well-paid sector of US workers, which is why airline unions have historically backed similar measures.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it never received a hearing or a vote, and the Congress ended without any action.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on May 18, 2023, joined by Senator Roger Marshall.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No further action was taken: the committee never voted on it and it never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign airlines using low-wage, foreign-based crews, which keep unrestricted access to the US market without a labor-standards review, and any travelers who benefit from the resulting fare competition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign carriers with low-wage crew models

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to add labor standards to foreign air carrier permit decisions.

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it one Republican cosponsor.

for.name: US airline labor unions
for.role: Backers of prior Fair and Open Skies proposals
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed the Fair and Open Skies concept as a way to protect US pilots and crews from labor-cost arbitrage by foreign carriers.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled it for consideration, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction (one Democrat and one Republican), but with only two senators backing it and no committee action or votes, no party-line pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: US airlines and their pilot and flight attendant unions
industries.note: A labor-standards review of foreign carrier permits would protect US airline crews' wages and level the field against airlines that base crews in low-wage countries. The benefit accrues to a specific workforce rather than workers generally, and could cost travelers through higher fares.

industries.industry: Foreign air carriers (including Gulf and European carriers)
industries.note: Carriers that keep costs down by hiring crews under foreign labor rules would face permit scrutiny that could raise their costs or limit their US access. Their competitive advantage comes partly from labor terms US carriers cannot match.
